extracted.intended_audience: painters, art students, and art critics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for perceiving, selecting, and rendering truthful visual facts in painting (priority of form over color; importance of characteristic and rare truths; role of moral sensibility and prior knowledge). Advice aimed at guiding artists' choices when they cannot render every detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility (bodily and moral) as basis for perception of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily sensibility to color and form is intimately connected with a higher sensibility (love, veneration) which sharpens perception and judgment; moral energy quickens perception and tempers judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception and judgment are 'so sharpened and brightened' when energized by moral feelings that a person with 'deadened moral sensation is always dull in his perception of truth.' Cultivate love, gratitude, veneration and other pure moral feelings to bring perceptive faculties into more effective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection and memory are necessary for retention and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Next to sensibility come reflection and memory, which are necessary for retention of impressions and recognition of their resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receive impressions and then reason upon them and trace them to their sources; without reflection one may misattribute impressions or invent causes. Strong imagination without reflection makes one 'see whatever he expects' and judge with feeling rather than with actual sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight depends upon previous knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: We are 'constantly supposing that we see what we know, and vice versa in their not seeing what they do not know.' The eye without knowledge is unreliable to discover truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train observation to detect facts not previously known (children draw a house as a T because of lack of knowledge). Teach the eye through repeated, close attention to perceive actual appearances rather than preconceived notions; beware painting 'what exists, rather than what they can see.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition often relies on least important attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: People recognize objects by their least important attributes (bindings of books, smell for dogs, coat for tailor), so recognition is not proof of real intrinsic resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake recognizability for truthful representation of essential characteristics; an image can be instantly recognized yet lack the higher truths (expression, spirit) that make it truly like the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: When unable to render all truths, preserve the most important
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist who cannot render all truths is most truthful who 'has preserved the most important at the expense of the most trifling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which truths are most characteristic of the subject and sacrifice minor details rather than essential characteristics; prioritize truths that define the species or individuality of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic (distinctive) truths determine importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Truths are important in proportion as they are characteristic of the thing of which they are affirmed; distinctiveness, not universality, renders a truth important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select truths that separate the species from everything else (what makes 'drapery' drapery), and then those that distinguish individuals; evaluate importance by how much an attribute defines the subject's identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular truths in predicate often outweigh general truths
rubrics_metrics.description: The aphorism 'General truths are more important than particular ones' is misleading in art; generality gives importance to the subject, whereas particularity in the predicate is key for painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the particular, characterizing predicate that conveys the subject's individuality (Turner's variety) over mere repetition of general themes (Claude/Poussin repetition). Consider whether a truth is predicate- or subject-general when deciding its value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truths of species are valuable because they tend toward beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Truths of species often represent perfection of form, and are therefore more intrinsically beautiful than many individual variations which may be defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a truth of species is also a beauty, it gains additional weight. Balance the search for individual character with appreciation for species-qualities that convey beauty and perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not represent accidental violations of nature's principles as norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature sometimes violates her principles rarely (instantaneous blemishes), but the artist who seeks after such violations exclusively is 'false to nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making aberrations the rule (e.g., painting only curved clouds because one month shows rounded clouds). Use rare violations sparingly and only when they serve a true purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek rare and evanescent manifestations of nature's powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist ought to watch for and arrest 'evanescent passages of perfected beauty'—those rare, striking manifestations in which nature's general powers are most perfectly shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue variety and novelty: give examples of nature's principles in their most peculiar and striking forms. The deeper the research and rarer the phenomena illustrated, the more valuable the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetition; variety is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: All repetition is blamable; to repeat the same effect in two pictures is 'wasted life'—the duty is to vary and present different lessons of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not repeat the same idea or effect across works; treat each composition as a singular sermon on one essential truth. Repetition is likened to a parrot-painter and considered treachery to nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize form (bulk, figure, light and shade) over color
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Locke: primary qualities (bulk, figure, number, situation, motion/rest) are characteristic of bodies; color is a secondary quality and therefore less important than form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render outline and chiaroscuro (light and shade) as the means by which form is explained to the eye. Do not sacrifice form to achieve color effects; consider form (including chiaroscuro) as the principal element in landscape and figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color is a secondary, changeable, and unreliable characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Color is changeful with season and light and is dependent on association; it is not a definitive characteristic of species or individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating color as the defining truth of an object (an oak is an oak regardless of leaf color). Because color depends on surrounding colors and the observer, prioritize properties less subject to variation (form, light and shade).

rubrics_metrics.name: Render drapery and accessory details unobtrusively when they distract
rubrics_metrics.description: When fabric or accessory details would draw attention from the principal subject (e.g., drapery on a Madonna), they should be suggested simply and sparely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give only those essential qualities necessary to identify the drapery; reject texture and ornate detail that draw the mind to dress rather than the saint. Example anti-patterns: an 'unlucky tassel' spoiling Canova's Perseus; unnecessary richness degrading a Madonna.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to represent the spirit (soul/moment) rather than mere bodily accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: A portrait can be faithful in feature yet lack expression, or it can capture a transient, high moment of the spirit which reveals the subject's deepest attributes; the latter is often more truthful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to catch moments where the soul's latent forces are revealed—'the call and claim of some divine motive'—rather than merely accurate bodily accidents. Such representations will be known only to those who have witnessed those moments and are of higher truth-value.
